definition: Aggrandize means to increase or make greater, especially one's own power or reputation.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word aggrandize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know aggrandize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every hallway portrait and gold-plated plaque at headquarters seemed designed to aggrandize the chief executive rather than honor the staff.
Flatter stops short of aggrandize — a flatterer wants a smile in the moment, while aggrandizing builds monuments, titles, and legend around its subject.
Deify goes further than aggrandize — it does not merely enlarge a leader's reputation but treats the leader as a god beyond question.

To glorify something is to praise it as glorious — to surround it with honor and admiration in words and ceremony. Aggrandize works on the thing itself, inflating its actual power or status, often past what was earned. Glorify changes how people talk about its subject; aggrandize changes how much its subject controls.

To elevate is to raise someone's rank or standing by legitimate means — a promotion that was earned. Aggrandize is elevation gone crooked: the rise is engineered, usually by the person rising, and it outruns anything deserved. If the new height was fairly won, say elevate; if it was manufactured, say aggrandize.

Aggrandize is sharper than 'praise' or 'build up' because it names the inflating of power or reputation beyond what was earned — the growth is engineered, and usually self-serving.
Aggrandize carries an edge of accusation — it hints that the growth in power or fame was engineered rather than earned.
For neutral growth say 'increase' or 'build up'; reach for aggrandize when someone is inflating a reputation, especially their own: the phrase self-aggrandizing is its most common modern form.

The Harlan wing was a gift, the museum's press release said, though the staff soon learned what the gift required.
Every gallery had to carry the donor's name, his portrait was hung at the entrance twice life-size, and two board seats passed to his nephews.
Older trustees grumbled that Harlan used philanthropy to aggrandize himself, trading paintings for power the bylaws never meant a donor to hold.
The curators counted quietly: exhibition choices now needed his approval, and his approval favored artists he owned.
The wing was beautiful; the arithmetic of control behind it was not.
